title: Contractor Overhead Calculator
description: Work out your overhead per hour and overhead percent, with a full cost list, worked job example, and a checklist to use today.

cover.alt: Illustration of a pie chart on a for pros blueprint background with a measuring tape

takeaways: Overhead per hour is your yearly overhead divided by your yearly billable hours, not hours worked.
In the worked example below, $31,200 of yearly overhead over 1,560 billable hours is $20.00 per hour.
If overhead is missing from a quote, the job pays your costs out of your profit.
body:
Your overhead per hour is your total yearly overhead divided by your billable hours for the year. Get that one number right and every quote you send covers the truck, the insurance, and the phone, not just the job in front of you. Most small firms that feel busy but broke have never done this sum.

## The formula for overhead per hour and overhead percent

Use two formulas. They answer two different questions.

**Overhead per hour = Total yearly overhead / Yearly billable hours**

**Overhead percent = Total yearly overhead / Yearly revenue x 100**

The per hour figure is the one you add to a job. The percent figure is the one you watch over time. If the percent creeps up year after year, your costs are growing faster than your sales.

Billable hours are hours you can charge to a customer. They are not paid hours. Drive time, quoting, bookkeeping, callbacks, and days lost to rain do not bill. A solo owner who works 40 hours a week for 48 weeks has 1,920 paid hours. If 20 percent of that time is not billable, billable hours are 1,536. Spreading overhead over 1,920 hours by mistake makes your rate too low on every job.

This sits next to your labor rate, not inside it. Our [contractor hourly rate calculator](/blog/contractor-hourly-rate-calculator/) builds your charge out rate. This page gives you the overhead part of that rate.

## Worked example: a two person painting firm

Say you run a small painting firm. Here are your monthly overhead costs, the costs you pay even in a week with no work.

| Monthly cost | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Insurance, liability and workers comp | $400 |
| Vehicle payment, fuel share, and repairs | $750 |
| Phone and data | $100 |
| Software, estimating and accounting apps | $150 |
| Shop or storage rent | $700 |
| Marketing and website | $300 |
| Accounting, licenses, and fees | $200 |
| **Total per month** | **$2,600** |

Step 1, yearly overhead. $2,600 x 12 = $31,200 per year.

Step 2, billable hours. You and one painter bill 130 hours a month between you on real jobs. 130 x 12 = 1,560 billable hours per year.

Step 3, overhead per hour. $31,200 / 1,560 = $20.00 per billable hour.

Step 4, check it the other way. $20.00 x 1,560 = $31,200. The full year of overhead is recovered. Good.

Step 5, overhead percent. Your yearly revenue is $156,000. $31,200 / $156,000 x 100 = 20 percent. One dollar in five goes to overhead.

Step 6, use it on a job. A house interior takes 24 billable hours. Overhead for that job is 24 x $20.00 = $480. Direct costs are $1,320 in labor and $480 in paint and materials, so $1,800. Total cost is $1,800 + $480 = $2,280. For a 15 percent profit margin, price = $2,280 / (1 - 0.15) = $2,280 / 0.85 = $2,682.35. Quote $2,685, rounded up.

Check step 6 by percent. 15 percent of $2,685 is $402.75. $2,685 - $402.75 = $2,282.25, close to the $2,280 cost, with the small gap from rounding the quote up. The math holds.

If you had quoted $1,800 plus profit and skipped overhead, the $480 would have come out of your pay. That is the whole point of this calculator. For the markup side of the same job, see our [markup vs margin calculator](/blog/markup-vs-margin-calculator/).

## What counts as overhead, and what does not?

Overhead is any cost that does not belong to one job. Use this checklist and tick off your own list today.

- Insurance: liability, workers comp, vehicle insurance
- Vehicles: payments, fuel, repairs, tires, registration
- Rent: shop, storage unit, office, yard space
- Phone, internet, and software subscriptions
- Marketing: website, ads, lead services, signs, wraps
- Accounting, bookkeeping, payroll service, legal fees
- Licenses, permits for the business, training, safety gear that is not job specific
- Small tools, ladders, sprayers, and equipment replacement
- Office supplies, uniforms, bank and card fees

Not overhead: paint, materials, and labor hours spent on a named job. Those are direct costs. Permit fees for one address are direct too. Your own target pay is not overhead either. It belongs in your labor rate. Mixing pay into overhead hides what the business really costs to run.

Go through last year bank and card statements line by line. Small subscriptions hide there. A $40 app you forgot is $480 a year, and at 1,560 billable hours it adds about $0.31 to every hour you sell.

## How do you find your real billable hours?

Track two weeks honestly before you guess. Write down start and stop times for billable work only. Most owners find 60 to 80 percent of paid time is billable.

A simple yearly method works too. Start with weeks you plan to work, say 48. Multiply by crew billable hours per week at full pace, say 65 for a two person crew with an owner who also quotes and runs jobs. That is 3,120 hours at full pace. Then cut it for weather, gaps between jobs, and slow months. At 50 percent use, you get 1,560, the figure in the example above.

Recheck this number each winter. One new hire, one lost contract, or a move to bigger jobs changes it, and a stale billable hour count quietly breaks every quote. Pair the new rate with our [painting estimate calculator](/blog/painting-estimate-calculator/) if you price paint work, or the [handyman pricing calculator](/blog/handyman-pricing-calculator/) for small jobs.

## Common overhead mistakes that cost you money

The first mistake is using paid hours instead of billable hours. It lowers your rate and spreads the loss across the whole year.

The second is leaving out once a year bills. Insurance premiums, license renewals, and accountant fees at tax time are easy to forget in a monthly list. Divide yearly bills by 12 and add them in.

The third is never updating. Rent goes up, fuel moves, a second truck arrives. Run this math at least once a year, and again any time a big fixed cost changes. A rate set three years ago is a pay cut you gave yourself.

The fourth is hiding overhead in a higher markup and hoping it works out. Hope is not a system. A per hour figure shows up on every quote, in the open, where you can defend it.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a normal overhead percent for a small contractor?
There is no single right figure, because rent, crew size, and area differ. Many small firms land between 15 and 35 percent of revenue. What matters is that your percent is based on your real costs, and that your prices recover it in full.

### Should I use overhead per hour or overhead percent on quotes?
Use per hour for labor heavy work, because hours drive most of your costs. Use percent as a check at the end of the job. If a finished job shows overhead well above your percent, your hours estimate was off.

### Does overhead include my own pay?
No. Your pay for work on a job is direct labor. Your pay for quoting and office time is covered because those hours are not billable, which is why billable hours are lower than paid hours. Do not count your wage twice.

### How often should I recalculate my overhead rate?
At least once a year, and any time insurance, rent, vehicles, or crew size change. In the example above, a $200 a month rent rise adds $2,400 a year. Over 1,560 hours, that is $1.54 more per hour on every quote.

### What if I work from home with no rent?
Then your overhead is lower, and that is fine. Use your real list, not a list copied from a bigger firm. Skip rent, keep insurance, vehicle, phone, software, and marketing. A lower true rate lets you price sharp and still make money.

## Next step
Put your new overhead figure into your next quote, then read our [free estimate template](/blog/free-estimate-template/) to lay that quote out clean.
